                    ### Question
                    A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of fatigue and pruritus. Examination of the abdomen shows an enlarged, nontender liver. Serum studies show an alkaline phosphatase level of 140 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase activity of 18 U/L, and alanine aminotransferase activity of 19 U/L. Serum antimitochondrial antibody titers are elevated. A biopsy specimen of this patient's liver is most likely to show which of the following findings?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Fibrous, concentric obliteration of small and large bile ducts
opb. Intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions in hepatocytes and cellular swelling
opc. Macrovesicular fatty infiltration and necrosis of hepatocytes
opd. Ballooning degeneration and apoptosis of hepatocytes
ope. Lymphocytic infiltration of portal areas and periductal granulomas
"

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of a 38-year-old woman with fatigue, pruritus, and an enlarged, nontender liver, along with elevated alkaline phosphatase and positive antimitochondrial antibodies, is highly suggestive of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). In PBC, liver biopsy typically reveals lymphocytic infiltration of portal areas and periductal granulomas, which aligns with the consensus on the histopathological findings associated with this autoimmune liver disease. Other options, such as fibrous obliteration of bile ducts or hepatocyte degeneration, do not correspond with the expected findings in PBC. Therefore, the most likely biopsy finding in this case is lymphocytic infiltration of portal areas and periductal granulomas.
